name: Essence
plain_explanation: Philosophers after Aristotle spoke of a thing's 'essence' -- the properties it cannot lose without ceasing to be itself -- but Russell argues this is really just a fact about how we choose to use a name, not a fact about the world: whether 'being a man' is essential to Socrates depends only on whether we would still call him 'Socrates' if that changed.
precise_definition: Aristotle's notion, central to the Posterior Analytics's account of definition and first premisses, that a thing's essential properties are those it cannot change without losing its identity, as opposed to accidental properties (like being happy or sad) that it can change while remaining the same thing; Russell calls this 'a hopelessly muddle-headed notion' whose real content is purely linguistic.
why_it_mattered: Essence became, per Russell, 'an intimate part of every philosophy subsequent to Aristotle... until we come to modern times,' making its critique essential to understanding a huge stretch of the later philosophical tradition, even though Russell judges the underlying concept confused.
historical_origin: Developed in Aristotle's Posterior Analytics as the basis for definitions and, ultimately, for the unproved first premisses all demonstration must start from.
examples: Socrates may be sometimes happy, sometimes sad -- accidental properties -- but it is supposed to be of his essence that he is a man, 'though a Pythagorean, who believes in transmigration, will not admit this.'
objections: Russell: 'the question of "essence" is one as to the use of words'; 'the "essence" of Socrates thus consists of those properties in the absence of which we should not use the name "Socrates."' A word may have an essence, but a thing cannot.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Persisted as a core philosophical concept for roughly two thousand years, per Russell, until displaced in modern philosophy.
